newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia seen on track for healthy trade surplus.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia seen on track for healthy trade surplus.

text.p: The Indonesian economy remained on track to maintain single-digit inflation and a healthy trade surplus through 1996, officials said on Wednesday.

Information Minister Harmoko said Indonesia's consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.41 percent in October following a decline of 0.04 percent in September. Year-on-year inflation was 6.56 percent in October, compared with 6.79 percent the previous month.
Harmoko said Indonesia had a trade surplus of $937.89 million in August, compared with $508.5 million in July.
"Month-on-month inflation in October was 0.41 percent. We consider it quite low. Food prices fell 0.04 percent," Harmoko told reporters following the monthly cabinet meeting devoted to the economy.
He said increases in the prices of housing, services and textiles had allowed inflation to edge up despite a drop in food prices.
"The president (Suharto) has ordered further tightening to get inflation lower. I think inflation will be below seven percent for this year," Harmoko said.

Total exports, including oil and gas, rose to $4.32 billion in August from $4.06 billion in July. Imports fell slightly to $3.38 billion from $3.55 billion during the same period. Oil and gas exports accounted for $971.49 million in August compared with July's figure of $909.7 million.
"We will continue to expand our non-oil exports. We will try to tap new markets in Latin America," Industry and Trade Minister Tunky Ariwibowo said.

The London-based research institute IDEA said the trade figure meant that over the first eight months, Indonesia's cumulative trade balance measured $3.92 billion, 66.2 percent up over the same period last year.
"As such, the full year trade surplus is on course to post its first year-on-year increase since 1993," it said.

IDEA said the trade figure would have the effect of strengthening the rupiah. The rupiah has enjoyed strong support this year on healthy fundamentals and attractive interest rate differentials compared with other exotic currencies.
Morgan Stanley said in a report that a recovery of domestic and foreign investment since 1994 was laying the foundation for medium-term economic growth of around 8.5 percent.
"The adoption of a more flexible exchange rate policy should enable the authorities to reduce inflation to five percent from the 9-10 percent average of recent years," it added.
It said Indonesia's commitment to lower inflation to five percent was a central feature of the medium-term scenario.
"The easiest way to maintain low and stable inflation is by a stable exchange rate policy. Thus we project the rupiah will remain relatively stable over the medium-term," it said.
